title: Namdev
hook: a boy sets a bowl of milk before the god, and waits for him to drink

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jnaneshwar for the last time. The yogi on the tiger, the children on the willing wall, and a book that ends by asking good for all beings.
screen: `JNANESHWAR.` · `A WALL ONLY HAS TO BE WILLING.`

segments.voice: A bowl of milk sits on the temple floor at Pandharpur, before the image of Vitthal, the dark god who stands on a brick with his hands on his hips. A small boy has carried it there. His father usually brings the offering, but he's away, so today the boy has been sent. He sets it down, folds his hands, and waits. The god doesn't move. The milk doesn't move. The boy keeps waiting. Nobody has told him that offerings are usually received unseen.
screen: `A BOWL OF MILK FOR VITTHAL.` → `A BOY SETS IT DOWN.` → `HE WAITS FOR THE GOD TO DRINK.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Namdev grew up in a family of tailors devoted to Vitthal, the form of Krishna worshiped at Pandharpur, whom his devotees call by tender names like Vithoba and, sometimes, mother. As the story goes, the boy waits, and still the god doesn't drink. So he pleads. He's done what his father does; why won't you take it? Is something wrong with me? Some tellings say he cries; some say he threatens to break his own head on the stone floor if Vitthal refuses. And Vitthal, the story says, reaches out of the image and drinks the milk. All of it. The boy goes home with an empty bowl, and nobody believes him. It's a funny story, and it knows it. But for Namdev, the god isn't an idea, and the offering isn't a gesture. If you bring a friend milk, the friend drinks it. He takes Vitthal at his word, the way a child takes anyone at their word, and the story rewards him instead of correcting him. Namdev grows up to be a singer. His songs, called abhangs, are short devotional poems in which he talks to Vitthal like someone in the same room: pleading, teasing, complaining, longing. In the Varkari tradition, people still sing abhangs, Namdev's among them, in kirtan, call and response, with cymbals keeping the beat. Jnaneshwar gave the people the Gita in their own language. Namdev gives them something smaller and just as bold: permission to treat God like someone who might actually drink the milk.
screen: `A FAMILY OF TAILORS, DEVOTED TO VITTHAL.` · `WHY WON'T YOU TAKE IT?` · `VITTHAL DRINKS THE MILK.` · `ABHANGS: TALKING TO GOD IN THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up, as if holding a small bowl, and think of something simple you could offer today: a glass of water, your full attention, a meal. Offer it the way the boy did, as if it will really be received, and don't rush the waiting. If you pray, offer it to God, by Vitthal's name or any name you already use.
Namdev. The tailor's son of the Marathi saint tradition, who, the story says, waited until Vitthal drank the milk, and grew up singing abhangs.
Your line: the bowl of milk. He simply expected it to be received. Day nine hundred sixteen, done.

howItsDone: Varkari devotees sing abhangs, including Namdev's, in kirtan with cymbals, and the temple of Vitthal at Pandharpur keeps a step at its entrance named for Namdev.
